summary: Damien Bohler's article on Permaculture Design in 5 Steps (published September 5, 2017 on permaculturenews.org) explains permaculture as a human-centred, integrated, ecologically harmonious method of designing landscapes. It outlines five design processes: mainframe design (water, access, structures, prioritised in that order), sector analysis of incoming energies such as sun, wind and fire, zone planning from Zone 0 to Zone 5, workflows (which the author calls lifeflows), and analysing and connecting components, illustrated with the chicken example. The note is truncated before the end of the component-analysis section.
one_line: A 2017 permaculturenews.org article by Damien Bohler outlining five permaculture design steps: mainframe, sector analysis, zone planning, workflows and component analysis.
key_facts: Damien Bohler's article 'Permaculture Design in 5 Steps' is dated September 5, 2017 and estimated at 21 minutes reading time.
The article describes permaculture design as an essentially multi-faceted, integrated and ecologically harmonious method of designing human-centred landscapes.
The article lists five design elements: Mainframe Design, Sector Analysis, Zone Planning, Workflows, and Analysing & Connecting Components.
Mainframe design features are, in order of approach: water, access and structures.
The permaculture water approach is summarised as 'slow, spread and sink'.
The article states that water design comes first because water will be the primary limiting factor on a site's ability to support life.
Access rules of thumb include crossing valleys along dam/pond walls, traversing the landscape on contour, and ascending and descending along ridge lines.
Sector analysis deals with consistent incoming energies to a site, such as sun, wind, rain, flood zones, fire danger, noise and pollution.
Zone planning radiates from Zone 0, the central habitation area usually the main house, with Zone 1 having the highest consistent need for attention and Zone 5 the wilderness zone.
Zone 4 is often thought of as 'farm forestry' and should require minimal yearly maintenance, possibly attention only several times a year.
The author prefers to call workflows 'lifeflows' because permaculture implementation creates an entire lifestyle.
The article states that the Permaculture Design Certificate (PDC) or equivalent training is currently taught as a 72 hour training course.
The author says that poor tool shed placement guarantees tools are left in the field and neglected, which the author treats as a design issue rather than a people issue.
The chicken is given as the common example in the Designers Manual and on PDCs for analysing components by listing needs, products and behaviours.
The author believes permaculture will eventually be taught in universities and even schools.
